structures.can_do: Can use 'but' to join a limited range of common adjectives, after 'be'.
structures.example: The weather was cloudy but fine. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'and' to join a limited range of common adjectives.
structures.example: The teachers are very nice and friendly . (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of compound adjectives ('up-to-date', 'state-of-the-art')
structures.example: The selling point is that it contains the most up-to-date and state-of-the-art know-how, for instance a water-proof keyboard, information security system, etc. A survey of our customers last year indicated that over 70% of them are content with the user-friendly designs. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Fail)

structures.guideword: FORM: COMBINING MORE THAN TWO ADJECTIVES
structures.can_do: Can use commas and 'and' to join more than two adjectives, after 'be'.
structures.example: Her name is Cassia, she is beautiful, intelligent, funny and very reliable. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: COMBINING THE SAME COMPARATIVE ADJECTIVE WITH 'AND'
structures.can_do: Can use 'and' to repeat a comparative adjective to indicate change over time, usually after 'become' or get. ► adjectives: comparatives
structures.example: I could see how the fire was burning the door, and the room became hotter and hotter. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a comma to combine two adjectives used before the noun, following the usual order of adjective types.
structures.example: It was the biggest TV in the bazaar, with its huge, black screen. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of compound adjectives ('good-looking', 'well-known')
structures.example: He was tall and good-looking. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'and' to join a limited range of comparative adjectives.► adjectives: comparatives
structures.example: In the winter you can go to the fitness centre, there you can get stronger and fitter. (Switzerland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Swiss German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adjective phrases to modify nouns.
structures.example: Besides, we could leave one day in the morning and travel by boat to a small and exotic island full of different and exotic species of birds that we could observe and photograph. (Turkey; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of compound adjectives ('open-minded', 'above-mentioned', 'well-to-do', 'jaw-dropping')
structures.example: I would describe myself as an easy-going and open-minded person. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a list of adjectives in ellipted clauses before and after a noun, to give focus. ► focus
structures.example: Imaginative, good-humoured, friendly, he was respected and liked by his peer-students. (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine more complex, lengthy strings of adjectives, joining the last two adjectives with 'and'.
structures.example: A timid, shy, self-conscious, over-sensitive and vulnerable person can yearn to make friends with someone who is very self-assured, confident, decisive, even bossy. (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1999; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form comparative adjectives with adjectives of two syllables ending in '-y' by changing the 'y' to an 'I' and adding '-er'.
structures.example: I like it because it's small and easier to use than other phones. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use comparative adjectives attributively, before nouns.
structures.example: I just watched a cricket match with my younger brother and my father. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Hindi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form comparative adjectives from adjectives of one syllable by adding '-er'.
structures.example: I played computer games with my older brother. (Vietnam; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a range of comparative adjective phrases using 'more' + longer adjectives (usually three or more syllables).
structures.example: I think you must be more careful. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form comparative adjectives with adjectives of one syllable ending in 'e', by adding '-r'.
structures.example: [talking about an alternative plan] I think it will be nicer. (France; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use comparative adjectives as a complement of 'be'.
structures.example: Sam, It would be better if you came after 4.30 p.m. (Sri Lanka; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Singhalese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form irregular comparative adjectives.
structures.example: What colour do you think is better? (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Spanish - Other; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form comparative adjectives with adjectives of one syllable with a short vowel, by doubling the final consonant and adding '-er'
structures.example: The rooms are all very beautiful, but I prefer my room because is bigger. (Italy; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2000; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'and' to repeat a comparative adjective to indicate change over time, usually after 'become' or 'get'.  ► adjectives: comparatives
structures.example: I saw everything become smaller and smaller. (China; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use '(so) much' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used predicatively after a verb, usually 'be'.
structures.example: I think the teacher in the new class is much better than the last one. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'a (little) bit' to modify comparative adjectives used predicatively after a verb, usually 'be'.
structures.example: He's 15, a bit smaller than me, dark hair, brown eyes. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a comparative adjective with 'than' to compare two nouns or noun phrases.► comparative clauses
structures.example: It's smaller than my old phone and I like it because it has bluetooth and it isn't very expensive. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'slightly' to modify comparative adjectives to a small degree.
structures.example: I bought a new one, since the price of a second-hand one was slightly cheaper. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'no' / 'not any' with comparative adjectives to limit the scale of comparison. ► comparative clauses
structures.example: That is why we are not any happier than you were. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2005; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'even' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used predicatively after a verb, usually 'be' and 'get'.
structures.example: [talking about a series of films] I'm sure you've seen part one already, but part two was even better! (Thailand; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Thai; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'a lot' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used predicatively after a verb, usually 'be'.
structures.example: In addition, remember that a bike, even a good one, is a lot cheaper than a car. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'not that much' to modify comparative adjectives to a small degree. ► comparative clauses
structures.example: Although she is not that much older than I am, one could think there were quite a few years between us. (Netherlands; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'much' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used attributively before countable and uncountable nouns.
structures.example: Although it is a second-hand computer which one of my colleagues sold me, it is a much better investment than the bicycle, I think. (Germany; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'too' with common gradable adjectives.
structures.example: They aren't too expensive. They cost like £30. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form adjective phrases with a very limited range of adjectives + a prepositional phrase.
structures.example: I think swimming is good for my body. (China; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2002; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'too' + adjective + prepositional phrase
structures.example: I bought them because I noticed that most of my clothes were too small for me. (Japan; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Japanese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'very' with a limited range of common gradable adjectives.
structures.example: I like Croydon because it's very quiet and very nice. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; Farsi)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs of degree ('really', 'so', 'quite') with an increasing range of common gradable adjectives.
structures.example: It was sunny and really hot every day! (Argentina; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'too' before adjectives followed by 'to'-infinitive.
structures.example: He always told me that he was too busy to write a letter to me, his wife. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'enough' to modify adjectives.
structures.example: My room is big enough, there is a lot of space, and for this reason I will buy a stereo. (Greece; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adjective phrases attributively, before a noun.
structures.example: … my boss told me that at 10.15 am I have a very important meeting. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form adjective phrases with 'quite a' + adjective.
structures.example: I been thinking about your last letter for quite a long time and I came to the following conclusion. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2004; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'enough' after adjectives followed by 'to'-infinitive
structures.example: [talking about an arts festival] I was lucky enough to take part in it last November, and I enjoyed it immensely. (Mexico; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adjectives ('main', 'only') that limit the noun that they go before.
structures.example: …the main reason is that I am practising the language. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2002; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adjectives predicatively, after 'be'.
structures.example: Yes, I am free Monday morning. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2011; Romanian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adjectives attributively, before a noun. ► noun phrases
structures.example: We have a big garden and a small swimming pool. (Arabic - Other, A1 BREAKTHROUGH, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can form adjective phrases with 'rather a' + adjective, often in formal contexts.
structures.example: Films tend to be rather a simple art, while books are a thing to be enjoyed in a calmer way. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adjectives in 'as … as' and 'so … that' in comparative structures. ► comparative clauses
structures.example: Because our debates do not draw as large a number of students as the guest appearances, but are still enjoyed by a relevant number of students, we propose a change of focus for the events. (Sweden; C2 MASTERY; 2006; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify gradable adjectives with extreme adverbs of degree ('absolutely', 'extremely', 'incredibly', 'totally') to intensify their meaning.
structures.example: I am absolutely sure that it will attract even more attention. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2004; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adjectives predicatively, after 'be'.
structures.example: I like my home because my bedroom is big. (Turkish, A1 BREAKTHROUGH, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use adjectives with the prefix a- ('asleep', 'awake', 'alive', 'alone') predicatively only, after linking verbs.
structures.example: I was very nervious because I was  alone at the bus station … (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do:
Can use an increasing range of adjectives attributively, before a noun.
► noun phrases
structures.example: The main character in the programme is a journalist who is visiting the town. (Arabic - Meghreb, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2007)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adjectives predicatively, after linking verbs 'look' and 'feel'.
structures.example: It is black and it looks perfect. (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the irregular superlative adjective 'best' in the phrase 'my best friend'.
structures.example: She's my best friend. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the '–ed' form of a verb as an adjective, after a noun.
structures.example: First of all, I would recommend providing a wider range of films and introducing discussions after each film shown. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adjectives before a noun to express intensity.
structures.example: As a conclusion, I shall say that the major problem concerns the exam. (France; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adjectives as object complement after 'make'.
structures.example: That's something that makes me angry! (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2010; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the adjectives 'present', 'future', 'former' before a noun.
structures.example: I think we all are very concerned about the present situation. (Germany; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an adjective or adjective phrase after pronouns like 'something', 'nothing', 'somewhere', 'nowhere'.
structures.example: I like cooking and I want to cook something special. (Slovakia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Slovak; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of degree adjectives ('real', 'absolute', 'complete') before a noun to express intensity.
structures.example: When tourists arrive, there is no area to park. This is a real problem and our town is becoming very dangerous for children; every week there is an accident. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a limited range of complex noun phrases with a superlative adjective  + prepositional phrase, to talk about something unique.► noun phrases ►  clauses: comparison
structures.example: It is the biggest zoo in the world. (Hong Kong; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2001; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of prepositional phrases with 'of' after a superlative adjective, to refer to one thing within a set or part of a set.
structures.example: My teacher said that it was the best project of all. (Russia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2010; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use prepositional phrases with 'in' + singular name of a place after a superlative adjective.
structures.example: It's the biggest room in the house. (Italy; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2000; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form superlative adjectives using the '-est' suffix, with adjectives of one syllable, and with two-syllable adjectives ending in -y.
structures.example: The easiest way to get my house is by Underground. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a noun phrase with 'my' or 'your' + superlative adjective + noun, with a limited range of nouns and contexts. ► noun phrases
structures.example: I bought these clothes for my youngest brother .... (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form superlative adjectives with adjectives of one syllable with a short vowel, by doubling the final consonant and adding '–est'.
structures.example: … it's the biggest and oldest museum in Libya. (Libya; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2001; Arabic - Meghreb; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a noun phrase with 'the' + superlative adjective + noun. ► noun phrases
structures.example: It has the latest technology. (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form superlative adjectives using the suffix '-st' to adjectives ending in '–e'.
structures.example: I always watch the latest music videos from there. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2010; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form superlative adjectives by adding the suffix '-est', to adjectives of one syllable.
structures.example: … it's the biggest and oldest museum in Libya. (Libya; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2001; Arabic - Meghreb; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the' with a limited range of superlative adjectives without a following noun, when the noun is understood.
structures.example: My relatives gave me presents but the computer game was the best. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form an increasing range of complex noun phrases with a superlative adjective + prepositional phrase, to talk about something unique. ► noun phrases
structures.example: Yesterday was the most exciting day of my life! (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form superlative adjective phrases using 'the most', with longer adjectives of two or more syllables.
structures.example: We love football competitions because here in Uruguay football is the most popular sport. (Uruguay; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'THE BEST' WITH NOUN AND PRESENT PERFECT
structures.can_do: Can use 'the best' before a noun + present perfect to talk about a unique experience.
structures.example: It was the best birthday present I have ever had. (Iran; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Farsi; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: 'THE BEST' WITH NOUN AND  'TO-' INFINITIVE
structures.can_do: Can use 'the best' before a noun + 'to'-infinitive.  ► clauses: comparative
structures.example: Summer is the best time to visit Poland. (Poland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2004; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a postmodifier to make the superlative stronger in the structure superlative + postmodifier + noun.
structures.example: What is more, in order to increase sales of the new model to the highest possible level, the possibility of entering the Asian markets should be considered. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2005; Polish; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use the premodifer 'by far' to make a superlative adjective stronger.
structures.example: As you know, I've already visited almost fifty forests all over the world but I think this one is by far the most beautiful of all. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use '(one of) the' with an increasing range of superlative adjectives without a following noun, when the noun is understood.
structures.example: There have been so many embarrassing moments in my life. It's very difficult to pick the most embarrassing. (Sweden; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use superlative adjectives before a noun + 'to'-infinitive. ► clauses: comparative
structures.example: To be honest, I think that, to be in competition with other markets, we need to be updated and the easiest way to do it is to use computers. (Italy; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'one of the' before a superlative adjective, followed by a plural noun. ► noun phrases
structures.example: It was one of the best days of my life. (Colombia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form noun phrases with a range of determiners before a superlative adjective. ► noun phrases
structures.example: There, people wear their best clothes. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the slightest', 'the faintest' with a specific range of nouns to express the least amount possible, most frequently following a negative verb form.
structures.example: I should not end my relationship with Alex by phone, without giving him the slightest explanation. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a postmodifier to make the superlative stronger, in the structure superlative + noun + postmodifier ('possible', 'ever', 'by far').
structures.example: … we want to present ourselves in the best way possible. (Yugoslavia; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Serbian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use 'soon' in the phrases 'See you soon' and 'Get well soon', as a signing-off device.
structures.example: Take care. See you soon. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Turkish; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('here', 'there') to indicate place.
structures.example: My girlfriend is here with me. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Slovak; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs and adverb phrases ('so much', 'a lot') with verbs to indicate degree or intensity. ► determiners
structures.example: I am looking forward to seeing you so much! (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Japanese; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use 'really' and 'very much' with verbs expressing preference ('like', 'love'), for emphasis.
structures.example: I really like theatre and a classical music. (Poland; A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2010; Polish; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('also', 'so', 'however') to show a relationship between two clauses or sentences.
structures.example: I also bought some t-shirts. (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use 'very' to make adjectives stronger.
structures.example: He's a very good man. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Mandarin; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('always', 'sometimes') to talk about frequency.
structures.example: I like Dorchester's people, they are always very friendly and polite. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Russian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('yesterday', 'just', 'now', 'already',) to refer to the timing of an event.
structures.example: Yesterday I went shopping. (Hungary; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Hungarian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of manner adverbs and adverb phrases to modify how something happens.
structures.example: … both the players played well. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Tamil; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs ('usually', 'often', 'never', 'weekly') to talk about frequency.
structures.example: People usually try to eat their breakfast between 7 and 9 am. (A2 Polish)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of degree adverbs ('so', 'quite', 'too') to modify adjectives.
structures.example: I went to Vinpearland. It's so beautiful. (Vietnam; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('only', 'just') to focus on or point to something.
structures.example: [talking about  a class] It's only two hours. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs and adverb phrases ('first', 'then', 'after that') to order segments of discourse.

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs to refer to the timing of an event.
structures.example: Dear Kate, I went to the cinema with a new friend recently. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of manner adverbs and adverb phrases to modify how something happens.
structures.example: They are like my sisters. We go everywhere together. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('actually', 'unfortunately', 'of course', 'I’m sorry') to indicate an attitude or viewpoint.
structures.example: It's very nice that you're going to help me to paint my bedroom. Actually I want you to decide what colour that my room should be. (Thai, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2006)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs and adverb phrases ('near', 'far away', 'upstairs', 'downstairs') to indicate place.
structures.example: You can't go far away because I don't think your parents want to pay for it. (Netherlands; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Dutch; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use 'really really' with verbs and adjectives for emphasis.
structures.example: Oh, I really really like her very friendly and lovely smile. (Vietnam; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of degree adverbs ('a little', 'a bit') with verbs to indicate degree or intensity. ► determiners
structures.example: When I came to England, one year ago, I didn't know any English word, now I'm very happy because I don't speak very well but I can understand and speak a little. (Sri Lanka; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Mongolian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs ('maybe', 'perhaps') to indicate degrees of certainty.
structures.example: Or maybe we can walk to there, because it's not far from my house. (China; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs ('therefore', 'furthermore', 'otherwise') to show a relationship between two clauses or sentences.
structures.example: You don't like city's with a lot of people. Therefore I suggest you go to a small school in the countryside, near your new home. (Switzerland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; French; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of focusing adverbs ('particularly', 'especially') to point to or highlight something. ► adverbs: position
structures.example: I usually read in my free time but particularly in the evenings before I go to the bed. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2005; Italian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use adverbs as discourse markers to organise text.  ►  adverbs: position ►  Discourse markers
structures.example: Firstly, I advise you to visit both schools. (Libya; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Amharic; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of adverbs to indicate degrees of certainty.
structures.example: It was undoubtedly an unforgettable experience. (Portuguese, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 1993)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs ('completely', 'obviously', 'clearly', 'actually', 'luckily', 'honestly', 'sadly', 'basically', 'obviously', 'hopefully') to indicate an attitude or viewpoint.
structures.example: I am completely sure. (Spanish - European, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2009)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of manner adverbs to modify how something happpens.
structures.example: She realises that he is a very dangerous man and that she should take his warning seriously. (Sweden; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of stance adverbs (simply, truly, surely, apparently, naturally, surprisingly, inevitably, literally, exceptionally, frankly, clearly, amazingly, wisely, admittedly) to indicate an attitude or viewpoint, often in clause initial position.
structures.example: Obviously everybody has the right to be on a strike. (Spanish - Other, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 1993)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of adverbs and adverb phrases to refer to the timing of an event.
structures.example: I look forward hearing from you shortly and I thank you in advance. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 1998; Catalan; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of adverbs with adjectives to express degree or intensity.
structures.example: It deals with the friendship between two completely different men. (Germany; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; German; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs to indicate degrees of certainty.
structures.example: [talking about a film] And it will probably be on TV next month! (Russia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Russian; Pass)

structures.sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.can_do: Can use adverbs mid clause, to distance the writer from what they are saying.
structures.example: He came out from school at the age of 16, and joined the "Universidad xxx" - the best one in Chile, supposedly - to study Economics (Spanish - Latin American, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 1993)

structures.can_do: Can use 'very' to modify common gradable adjectives.
structures.example: My home is very nice. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Italian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: TIME  and SEQUENCING, MODIFYING CLAUSES
structures.can_do: Can use time and sequencing adverbs to modify clauses and sentences.
structures.example: Yesterday I went shopping and bought some clothes. (Russia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of manner adverbs to modify verbs.
structures.example: You have to choose carefully. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of manner adverbs to modify verbs.
structures.example: I really liked it because all the candidates were professional and swam very fast. (Argentina; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of degree adverbs to modify adverbs. ► adverb phrases: form
structures.example: We left really early on a Friday morning. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'very' to modify time adverbs. ► adverb phrases
structures.example: I hope you get well very soon. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Bengali; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use place adverbs ('here', 'there') as complements of verbs.
structures.example: I am happy here because people are very nice. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Hindi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs to modify clauses and sentences to indicate stance or attitude.
structures.example: But, obviously, you prefer going with your friends because you will have a better time. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of degree adverbs to modify common gradable adjectives.
structures.example: I'm so happy because you can come! (France; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; French; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: DEGREE and TIME, MODIFYING VERBS
structures.can_do: Can use degree and time adverbs to modify verbs.
structures.example: I really like Japanese music. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use degree adverbs ('slightly', 'a bit', 'much') to modify comparatives.
structures.example: My Spanish is slightly more fluent than my English, because I lived in Spain longer than in England. (Russia; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Russian; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use degree adverbs ('almost', 'very') to modify determiners. ► determiners
structures.example: Today, thanks to the Internet, I can work at home almost all the time, which is far more relaxing and less boring. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of adverbs in front position.
structures.example: Sometimes I go to the beach. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2011; Arabic - Other; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of degree adverbs to modify a range of adverb types. ► adjectives ► adverb phrases: form
structures.example: The attitude of young people today towards keeping fit and healthy has almost completely changed.  (Germany; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use degree adverbs to modify pronouns. ► pronouns
structures.example: You can eat very well and pay almost nothing. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of degree adverbs before an adjective.
structures.example: My home is very light and very comfortable. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use frequency adverbs in the usual mid position, between the subject and the main verb.
structures.example: In my free time I always listen to music, watch TV, clean my room ... (Spain; A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2010; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use degree adverbs to modify noun phrases. ► noun phrases
structures.example: It would be quite a formal meeting. (Thailand; B2 VANTAGE; 2001; Thai; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'really' in the usual mid-position, between the subject and the main verb.
structures.example: I really love walking. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2011; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use time adverbs in the usual end position.
structures.example: Get well soon. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Nepali; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use manner adverbs in the usual end position.
structures.example: Please answer me quickly because there are only eleven tickets. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2010; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs in mid position between the subject and the main verb and after modal verbs, auxiliary verbs and 'be'.
structures.example: I bought it because it is very pretty, but it wasn't expensive, I only spent thirty pounds! (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of degree adverbs before an adjective.
structures.example: I'm so glad you are coming. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of adverbs in front position.
structures.example: [talking about taking a language course] However I can study only on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, because I am working in the restaurant. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use place adverbs in the usual end position.
structures.example: I have many friends there. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Polish; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use degree adverbs in end position.
structures.example: I miss you a lot. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use evaluative, viewpoint and sequencing adverbs outside the clause, in front position, as a cohesive device to link to a previous statement in a preceding clause.
structures.example: It's very nice that you're going to help me to paint my bedroom. Actually I want you to decide what colour that my room should be. (Thai, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2006)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs in mid position, to distance the writer from what they are saying.
structures.example: In all actuality Piggy himself theoretically has all the necessary character traits and skills at his disposal that would ensure he would be an effective leader. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify an increasing range of adverbs with other adverbs.► adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
structures.example: We get along quite well. (Belgium; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'never' in front position followed by an inverted subject (most commonly 'I') + main verb verb, to give focus.
structures.example: Never have I seen such a realistic and impressive film before. (Argentina; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'hardly' in front position followed by an inverted subject and verb, to give focus.
structures.example: Hardly had he reached his front door when he heard the phone ringing. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify adverbs of time and degree with 'very'.
structures.example: I hope you will be fine very soon. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify a limited range of adverbs of time, degree, and manner with other adverbs.
structures.example: I love it so much. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can post-modify adverbs with 'enough to intensify'.
structures.example: Surprisingly enough, Meal's management was very responsive. (Netherlands; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2009; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify an adverb with a comparative structure.
structures.example: Obviously, you can get to work by car quicker and more comfortably than by bicycle. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify a wide range of adverbs with other adverbs.
structures.example: Even the beautiful, attractive cover and the extra Audio CD aren’t enough to justify the slightly higher price, especially because the value of this game will drop extremely rapidly. (Luxembourg; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can post-modify adverbs with a complex prepositional phrase complement, to highlight information.
structures.example: Luckily for you, I kept notes on everything we did, so I proudly present to you the top 4 of our course-days. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form adverb phrases with modifiers before, and complements after, adverbs.
structures.example: Many politicians and owners of big enterprises have been able for a long time to work almost exclusively for their own interests. (C2 MASTERY; 1993; ; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'than' + a finite clause forming the second part of a comparison after a comparative adjective
structures.example: I wish our schools could become better than they are. (Georgia (Republic of); B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Georgian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'than' + a limited range of non-finite clauses (with -ing), forming the second part of a comparison after a comparative adjective
structures.example: Well, If I were you I would go to a small school in the countryside because it's less complicated than going to a large school in a town. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'rather than' + noun phrase or prepositional phrase to stress one element in a comparison.
structures.example: Use the stairs rather than the lift, the bike rather than the tube and whenever you've got enough time, try running around the neighbourhood in the morning before going to work. (Colombia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use '(not) as' + adjective/adverb + 'as' to introduce a clause (often with a substitute auxiliary verb) to talk about two things being equal or unequal in some way.
structures.example: When I come back from the hospital, I will try to cover the work as much as I can. (Thailand; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Thai; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'like' + noun or pronoun.
structures.example: I like her because she is like me. (Poland; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2010; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'too' + adjective + 'to'-infinitive.
structures.example: First of all, I think you are too young to go on holiday by yourself. (Cyprus; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the best (that)' followed by a clause with the present perfect to talk about something unique.
structures.example: It's the best place that I have ever seen. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: 'THE SAME' (+ NOUN) + 'AS' + PRONOUN OR NOUN
structures.can_do: Can use 'the same' (+ noun) + 'as' + pronoun or noun.
structures.example: I wasn't the only one in my class, there were many others at the same level as me. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the same' (+ noun) + 'as' + clause.
structures.example: Maybe I'll do the same thing as you did. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'so' + adjective + 'that' clause.
structures.example: I was so tired that I didn't have the strength to stand up and ask him for a photograph. (Chile; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'enough' after adjectives followed by 'to'-infinitive.
structures.example: In my opinion young people at that age are not mature enough to decide by themselves what they want for their future. (B2 VANTAGE; 2009; German; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: SENSE VERBS + 'AS IF' OR 'AS THOUGH' + FINITE CLAUSE
structures.can_do: Can use verbs of the senses + 'as if' or 'as though' + finite clause.
structures.example: I was excited and I felt as if I was a bird. (Japan; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Japanese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use linking verbs + 'like' or 'similar to'.
structures.example: Some people have told me that I look like a pop star when I wear it. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a superlative adjective (+ noun) (+ 'that') followed by a clause to talk about something unique.
structures.example: It was probably the best comedy that anyone could ever have made; however, to the ones who were in the cinema, it didn't seem like a comedy but a horror film. (Portugal; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: .||Can use than + an increasing range of non-finite clauses (to-infinitive, reduced clause)  forming the second part of a comparison after a comparative adjective||
structures.example: It is much easier to be single than to have a partner. (B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'rather than' + a non-finite clause to stress one element in a comparison.
structures.example: If you prefer watching TV rather than reading, you have to be critical: you mustn't in any way accept everything, every image that passes in front of your eyes. (Portugal; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the best' as a superlative adverb + pronoun + ellipted 'can' or 'could'.
structures.example: I'm sorry to say that she is not the best of cooks but she tries the best she can. (Sweden; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: 'AS IF' OR 'AS THOUGH' + FINITE CLAUSE
structures.can_do: Can use 'as if' or 'as though' + finite clause to introduce a second clause as a comparison.
structures.example: Her heart beat extremely fast, as if it was going to burst out of her chest. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'so' + adjective + 'as' + 'to'-infinitive clause, usually in formal contexts.
structures.example: Travellers should not be so ignorant as to think they can understand other nationalities better when they have once lived in one of their hotels. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'as if' + non-finite clause to introduce a second clause as a comparison.
structures.example: She closed her eyes as if to push those thoughts away. (Brazil; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine multiple main clauses, with commas and conjunctions expressing order, often to give instructions or directions.
structures.example: Your house is near to mine so turn down the 5th street and then go straight almost all the way. When you see the purple street turn there, then go to the left to the Red street, that is my street, my house is 17. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine two main clauses of the same type using 'neither' in front or mid position, followed by 'nor' to introduce the second clause, for emphasis.
structures.example: We neither walk nor do exercises. (Turkey; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Turkish; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can omit the subject in a second main declarative clause when the subject is obvious or the same as the first clause.
structures.example: She likes to listen to music and watch TV. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine two main declarative clauses using co-ordinating conjunctions ('and', 'but', 'or').
structures.example: I like my college and I like my class. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Gujarati; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: COMBINING CLAUSES OF THE SAME TYPE
structures.can_do: Can combine clauses of the same type, main or subordinate, finite or non-finite, with conjunctions.
structures.example: You will have a great time with your friends, because I know they are going to the seaside and staying in a hotel near the sea. (Georgia (Republic of); B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Georgian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine multiple main clauses with a range of conjunctions, often in a narrative context.
structures.example: By the time his mother arrived home, the suitcase was still lost, so Larry decided to tell her the truth, but then his mother showed him his suitcase and told Larry that he left it in the car. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine two main clauses of the same type using 'either' in front or mid position, followed by 'or' to introduce the second clause.
structures.example: Regarding your future plans, we would like to know which city you are going to move to, so that if we get the chance, we can either visit you or write to you. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine clauses using 'not only' in mid position of the first clause followed by … 'but (also)' to introduce the second clause, to give focus.
structures.example: The atmosphere was friendly, not only because it wasn't too crowded, but also because the waiters always help you. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'NOT ONLY … BUT (ALSO)' WITH INVERSION, FOCUS
structures.can_do: Can combine clauses using 'not only' in front position followed by an inverted first clause + … 'but (also)' to introduce the second clause, to give focus.
structures.example: And not only did they come for the most popular sports, such as football and basketball, but many other less known activities were very well attended. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form simple affirmative declarative clauses.
structures.example: I study English at college. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Mandarin; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can combine a negative clause with an inverted clause with 'nor', to give focus.
structures.example: That night Kevin did not sleep; nor did Kristin. (Spain; C2 MASTERY; 1999; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a simple negative declarative clause with lexical 'be' + 'not' or 'n't'.
structures.example: My college is not very big. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form simple negative declarative clauses.
structures.example: I don't like maths. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Farsi; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: AFFIRMATIVE DECLARATIVE, MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS
structures.can_do: Can form an affirmative declarative clause with modal verbs.
structures.example: I can go to see her tomorrow. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Panjabi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form an affirmative imperative with the base form of a main verb.
structures.example: Goodbye. Write soon. (Russia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Russian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: NEGATIVE DECLARATIVE, MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS
structures.can_do: Can form a simple negative declarative clause with modal verb + 'not' or 'n't'.
structures.example: I know you couldn't come to my party so I want to tell you about my presents and party. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a simple negative declarative clause with auxiliary 'have' + 'not' or 'n't' and 'have' + 'not' or 'n't (got)'
structures.example: I haven't eaten Italian food for a long time. (Ecuador; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the auxiliary verb 'do' in an affirmative declarative clause, for emphasis and affirmation.
structures.example: Yes, I do have a favorite restaurant. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2005; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the imperative to give instructions.
structures.example: Take a taxi to the Petrol station then call me. (Libya; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Arabic - Meghreb; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use negative imperative after an instruction, for emphasis.
structures.example: Our house is next to the school and my home is opposite the post office. Don't forget. (Tamil, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use 'let's' + base form of a main verb, for first person plural imperatives to make a suggestion.
structures.example: The concert will be in Canecão. Let's go!!! (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a negative imperative with the auxiliary verb 'do' + 'n't' + base form of a main verb, to give advice, instructions or orders.
structures.example: Don't tell Lucy, please. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the imperative to give instructions, often at the end of a letter or when saying goodbye to someone.
structures.example: Email or phone me. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Estonian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'let's not' + base form of a main verb to make a suggestion.
structures.example: Let's not lose track of each other again! (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'do' + base form of a main verb, for emphasis or in formal contexts.
structures.example: Do write back and let me know all your news. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the imperative to make an offer or an invitation.
structures.example: Come and visit us after the New Year, we've got so much to talk about. (Somali, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can use an imperative clause with 'let me' + base form of a main verb, as a focusing device, to introduce something
structures.example: Let me tell you my story. (Taiwan; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'do not' for emphasis or in formal contexts.
structures.example: Do not forget to have a break at lunchtime and try to eat your meal whenever possible in a silent room. (Switzerland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'LET' + THIRD PERSON PRONOUN, DEVOLVING RESPONSIBILITY
structures.can_do: Can use an imperative clause with 'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to devolve responsibility.
structures.example: Let them find their own food. (Portugal; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'LET' + THIRD PERSON PRONOUN, PERMISSION, ORDER
structures.can_do: Can use an imperative clause with  'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to  give permission or allow something or instruct someone to allow something.
structures.example: Try to play chess with him whenever you can and remember: Let him win! (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use imperatives to point within or to a document within formal contexts, often academic.
structures.example: See enclosed brochure. (Sweden; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an imperative clause with  'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to disallow something or instruct someone to disallow something.
structures.example: Don't let them spend all their free time in front of the TV. (Sweden; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use imperatives to introduce a condition followed by 'and' to introduce a consequence of the condition.
structures.example: See one of them and you'll want to see them all. (C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: AFFIRMATIVE INTERROGATIVE, WITH MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS
structures.can_do: Can form interrogative clauses ('yes/no' forms) with modal auxiliary verbs.
structures.example: Would you like to come with me? (Argentina; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use you with an imperative form to make an instruction stronger.
structures.example: Don't you ever do that again! (Cyprus; C2 MASTERY; 2001; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form interrogative clauses ('yes/no' forms) with auxiliary 'be' and 'have'.
structures.example: Are you going to the new art class? (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form interrogative clauses with 'be'.
structures.example: How are you? (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Farsi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form interrogative clauses ('yes/no' forms) of main lexical verbs with auxiliary 'do'.
structures.example: Do you remember Julie? (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form 'wh-' interrogative clauses with a 'wh-' word as object.
structures.example: When are you coming here? (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'What a pity' + ('that') clause.
structures.example: What a pity that you didn't come. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'What a' + noun phrase and 'What a' + noun phrase + clause.
structures.example: What a brilliant idea. (France; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form questions with a 'wh-' word as subject, without an auxiliary verb.
structures.example: What happened? (Spanish - Latin American, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can form negative interrogative clauses with an adverb in mid position, between the subject and the main verb.
structures.example: Money - hasn't it always been one of the most important problems for students? (Japan; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Japanese; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can form interrogative clauses with an adverb in mid position, between the subject and the main verb.
structures.example: Have you ever been to Marseille? (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form negative interrogative clauses.
structures.example: Isn't it great? (Switzerland; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form negative 'wh-' interrogative clauses.
structures.example: Why don't we watch a film? (Sri Lanka; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Tamil; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'How' + adjective.
structures.example: How exciting! (China; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'How' + adjective + clause.
structures.example: How lucky you are to have visited that exhibition! (Switzerland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause with 'who' as the subject.
structures.example: It's about a girl who went to the war when she was 22 years old. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 1999; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause with 'which' as the subject.
structures.example: At the end of the game, the KASAS sang to Hagas a piece of music which makes me cry. Suzanna watched with me and she cried alot. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative interrogative form of an auxiliary verb to express surprise or enthusiasm.
structures.example: Wouldn't it be wonderful! (Russian, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause with 'that' as the object.
structures.example: The team that I like is called 'The Monkeys', but Paty prefers 'The Walls'. (Uruguay; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-defining relative clause with 'who' as the subject.
structures.example: I watched it with my brother who was also interested in sports. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'How' + clause.
structures.example: How I often longed to play with the other children or relax with a good book. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-defining relative clause with 'which' as the subject,.
structures.example: I bought it in Peter's Mobile shop, which is near to my home. (Sri Lanka; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Tamil; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'How' + adverb + clause.
structures.example: How differently we were brought up by our mother. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause with 'which' as the object.
structures.example: I came to your house yesterday with the computer game which I borrowed from Mayank. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Hindi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-defining relative clause with 'which' as the object.
structures.example: The best of all was a marble statue which my aunt gave me. (Bangladesh; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Bengali; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses, 'the person who/that, the thing that, the (only) one who/that' as a focusing device.
structures.example: The thing that was great is that the weather was really warm and it didn't rain. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses with 'where' to define nouns referring to place.
structures.example: The city where I live is very nice and extremely charming. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; ; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses with 'when' to define nouns relating to time.
structures.example: The day when he had to go back to Korea, I could not stop myself crying. (Korea, South; B1 THRESHOLD; 1999; Korean; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-defining relative clause with 'who' as the object.
structures.example: What I liked most was the friend I made there, a green-eyed chubby boy, who I played with till dinner time, when I had to go home. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause, without a relative pronoun.
structures.example: My friends said the clothes I wore were very old, and they didn't like them. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses and non-defining relative clauses ending in a preposition, with 'who/which/that' as the complement of the preposition.
structures.example: Thank you very much for having provided us with valuable information about your finance services, which we are greatly interested in. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses with 'why' after 'reason', to give an explanation and for focus.
structures.example: The reason why I love it is that it's quite original because it's about a woman who can see ghosts. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a defining relative clause with 'who' or 'that' as the object.
structures.example: My friends are the people who I love most. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining and non-defining relative clauses with 'whose name'.
structures.example: We have a new employee whose name is Mary Watts. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use non-defining relative clauses with 'whose', to give additional information.
structures.example: And I was initially employed to be an entrance assistant, whose job was to keep the queue under control as well as keeping the area clean. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use defining relative clauses with 'whose', to give more information about relationship.
structures.example: I visited several primary schools in Canberra and had opportunities to teach not only Australian children but also Vietnamese children whose parents immigrated to Australia. (Japan; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Japanese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with conjunctions ('even though, (al)though, while if') to introduce contrast, before or after a main clause.
structures.example: You should come with your sister even though you would rather be alone. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with 'because', after a main clause, to introduce reasons.
structures.example: I love her because she is friendly. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Bengali; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with conjunctions to introduce reasons, after a main clause.
structures.example: I prefer to speak on 14 July, as I have got another appointment on the next day. (India; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Malayalam; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a relative clause to refer to a whole clause or sentence, often to express an opinion or evaluation or give a reason.
structures.example: It is now possible to send a letter and receive an answer within ten minutes, which is a good thing if you want to buy a house, a car etc. (Denmark; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; Danish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with 'if', before or after a main clause, to introduce conditions. ► clauses: conditionals
structures.example: I would be very happy if you visit me in Dublin. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Spanish - Other; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with 'to', to introduce purpose.
structures.example: To get to my house you'll have to take the 5th avenue and go 6 streets to the left and at the bottom you'll see another street, go 3 streets to the right and there you'll find my house. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with time conjunctions, before or after a main clause.
structures.example: I feel comfortable when I am wearing these clothes. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Malay; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause with conjunctions ('so (that), in order that') to introduce purpose and result, after a main clause.
structures.example: I think it is important to write about this topic so that young students and other people who are working with business, can get some inspiration. (Sweden; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with 'after' + 'having/being' + '-ed' form, before a main clause, to refer to past time.
structures.example: After having worked for many hours, you'll probably be tired. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use a finite subordinate clause, before or after a main clause, with conjunctions to introduce conditions. ► clauses: conditionals
structures.example: Unless something is done many people will die. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with 'before' and 'after' + '-ing', before or after a main clause, to refer to time.
structures.example: Instead I buy books once a month and I read them in the evening before going to bed. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2005; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use non-finite clauses after 'if'. .► 'clauses: conditionals'
structures.example: Please do not hesitate to ask for further assistance if needed. (other; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'Were' + pronoun + 'to' infinitive to introduce a condition, in formal contexts.
structures.example: Were I to choose one of them, I would select the last one, so that I could have the opportunity to take part in my favourite radio station's programme. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2005; Greek; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with an '-ed' form, before a main clause, to give focus.
structures.example: Compared to the campsite job this one has its advantages. (Romania; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Romanian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use non-finite clauses after subordinating conjunctions '(although, though)', to express contrast.
Can introduce a subordinate clause with inverted 'should/had/were' + subject + verb, in formal contexts.
structures.example: Should you need any further assistance, do not hesitate to contact me. (Czech; Czech Republic; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; Pass; 2007)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite clause, introduced by 'not' + '-ing', to give more information.
structures.example: Not knowing the North of London very well it took me quite a long time to get there. (Germany; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2004; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite clause, introduced by '-ing' before a main clause, to give more information.
structures.example: Having no choice, I sat down on a bench which was in the middle of the road to wait for the rain to stop. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: PRESENT SIMPLE 'IF' CLAUSE + MODAL, FUTURE, POSSIBLE OUTCOME
structures.can_do: Can use 'if' + present simple to introduce a possible future condition, with modal verbs in the main clause, to talk about a possible result. ► modality
structures.example: I think that it would be very good if you start going to the gym or you start cycling. (Colombia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an 'if-' clause ('if you want', 'like', 'prefer') to soften the directness of imperatives, offers or suggestions.
structures.example: Bring some films if you want. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: PRESENT SIMPLE 'IF' CLAUSE, REAL CONDITIONS
structures.can_do: Can use 'if' + present simple with present simple, 'can' or imperative in the main clause to refer to things that are true now or very likely to happen.
structures.example: If I have spare time I always read a book. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Turkish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: PRESENT SIMPLE 'IF' CLAUSE + 'WILL', FUTURE, LIKELY OUTCOME (FIRST CONDITIONAL)
structures.can_do: Can use 'if' + present simple to introduce a possible future condition, with 'will' in the main clause to talk about a likely result.
structures.example: I talked to my parents and I think if you tell them your reasons, they will accept it. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'if' + present simple, with an imperative in the main clause.
structures.example: If you find it, call me. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form conditional subordinate clause with 'if' + present simple.
structures.example: It is 3 hours long, and if you want to pass it you will have to study very hard, it is very difficult. (Italy; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Italian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: PRESENT CONTINUOUS 'IF' CLAUSE , PLANS & ADVICE
structures.can_do: Can use 'if' + present continuous or 'going to' to introduce a possible plan, with modal verbs or imperatives in the main clause to give advice.
structures.example: Billy, if you are moving you should think a lot, first you have to go and see the two schools. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF' + PAST SIMPLE + 'WOULD', FUTURE, IMAGINED SITUATION|(SECOND CONDITIONAL)
structures.can_do: Can form conditional subordinate clauses with 'if' + past simple, and would in the main clause, to talk about an imagined situation, often in the context of advice or opinion-giving.
structures.example: Maybe it would be more fun if you went with your friends. (Portugal; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF' + PAST PERFECT + 'WOULD HAVE' + '-ED', IMAGINED SITUATION, REGRET|(THIRD CONDITIONAL)
structures.can_do: Can form conditional subordinate clauses with 'if' + past perfect simple and 'would have' + '-ed' in the main clause, to talk about imagined situations in the past, often with regret.
structures.example: If they had not been there, I would have been very lonely. (Vietnam; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF' + PAST SIMPLE + 'COULD', FUTURE, IMAGINED SITUATION
structures.can_do: Can form conditional subordinate clauses with 'if' + past simple, and 'could' in the main clause to talk about an imagined situation, often in the context of suggesting.
structures.example: If you wanted to do some outdoor activities, we could go fishing or even walking through the green fields. (Egypt; B1 THRESHOLD; 2004; Arabic - Egyptian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF I WERE YOU' + 'WOULD', FUTURE, IMAGINED SITUATION
structures.can_do: Can use 'if I were you' and 'would' in the main clause often in the context of advice or opinion-giving.
structures.example: Well, if I were you I would go to a small school in the countryside because it's less complicated than going to a large school in a town. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'unless' + present simple to talk about an exception, with present and future reference.
structures.example: I think I am going to pay by cash, unless you accept credit cards. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form ellipted 'if' clauses with 'if' + '-ed' form.
structures.example: Furthermore I found little rooms where an employee could take a short nap if needed. (Switzerland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2002; Swiss German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'If not' as a conditional clause to offer an alternative to refer to a previous direct or indirect 'yes-no' question where the answer might be ‘no’.
structures.example: Is the Sheraton Hotel ok for you? If not, call me as soon as possible. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'If so' as a conditional clause to refer a previous direct or indirect 'yes-no' question where the answer might be ‘yes’. ► Clauses coordinated
structures.example: Do you think we could have an extra class? If so, I'd like to do it to cover the work I'll miss. (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF' + PAST PERFECT + MODAL VERBS IMAGINED SITUATION, REGRET
structures.can_do: Can form conditional subordinate clauses with if + the past perfect simple and modal verb + 'have' + '-ed' in the main clause, to talk about imagined situations in the past, often with regret.
structures.example: All this could have been avoided, if the plan had been more flexible. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use conditional subordinate clauses with a range of conjunctions ('as long as', 'provided') + present simple or present continuous, with future reference.
structures.example: As long as it involves children I'd be delighted to work for you during the summer. (Denmark; B2 VANTAGE; 1998; Danish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form subordinate conditional clauses with 'if you should', in polite, formal contexts.
structures.example: If you should have any concerns about my choice, please tell me. (Germany; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: INVERTED PAST PERFECT, IMAGINED PAST
structures.can_do: Can use past perfect +  inverted subject, and a modal verb + 'have' + '-ed' in the main clause  to talk about imagined situations in the past.
structures.example: Had he been more experienced he would have known that these things always happen in this part of the world. (Sweden; C2 MASTERY; 2001; Swedish; Pass)

structures.guideword: USE: INVERTED 'SHOULD', FUTURE, POSSIBLE OUTCOME, FORMAL, POLITE
structures.can_do: Can use inverted 'should', + 'would' in the main clause to talk about possible future outcomes, in polite or formal contexts.
structures.example: Should we win your prize we would like to build a new school close to our production center, for the children of the area. (Switzerland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2004; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'Were it not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
structures.example: Were it not for my university, I would give up this class immediately. (Russia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'were' with an inverted subject + 'to' infinitive, to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
structures.example: Were I to win this travel scholarship, the country of my choice would be Japan. (Switzerland; C2 MASTERY; 2001; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use conditional subordinate clauses with a range of conjunctions ('so long as', 'on condition that', 'in the event that') with past, present or future reference.|
structures.example: As a matter of fact, education is free and as a result they can attend whichever university they desire so long as they have the proper qualifications, of course. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2005; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can introduce a conditional subordinate clause with 'should' + inverted subject.
structures.example: Should you require any further information about the program or any other detail please do not hesitate to ask for it. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2002; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF IT WERE NOT FOR', FORMAL
structures.can_do: Can use 'If it weren’t / were not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple
structures.example: If it weren't for that boy, I am definitely certain that I would have failed the examinations and I would have ended up taking the class again the following year. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'If it were' + 'to-' infinitive to introduce conditions in formal contexts.
structures.example: If it were to be published, the first issue would probably include a small introduction about the people who helped in the creation of the magazine. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2001; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'whether or not' to introduce conditions in formal contexts.
structures.example: Whether or not the visitors should imitate local customs and behaviour is definitely a debatable issue. (India; 2003; Hindi)

structures.can_do: Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine phrases.
structures.example: My home is very light and very comfortable. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine sentences.
structures.example: I like it because there are lots of shops, it is not too busy and there is lots of parking. And I like my home because it's not too big and it's a very nice flat. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Tamil; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'and' and 'or' before the final item in a list.
structures.example: I like to eat chicken, mushrooms and some vegetables. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to combine clauses.
structures.example: He is a journalist and he likes everything about cinema. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use single word conjunctions ('and, but, or') to connect single nouns and adjectives.
structures.example: I like chicken and rice. I don't like meat and fish. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Kurdish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'either … or' to connect two words, phrases or clauses.
structures.example: The men wear suits, either white or black, and the bride and women wear special long dresses, usually the same colour. (Yugoslavia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Serbian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'but' to add an unexpected contrast.
structures.example: I really like my home, it is very small but it is very easy to clean. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'plus' to connect clauses and sentences, often to point out a positive addition or advantage.
structures.example: I would be more than pleased to receive you at home, it's not too big, but we could have a lot of fun, plus you won't have to pay a thing! (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2004; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of conjunctions ('and, but, or, so, then') to combine more complex strings of clauses and sentences.
structures.example: I was scared and closed the window, but I couldn't sleep, so a few minutes later I opened the window again, but they were gone. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'plus' as coordinating conjunction, often in relation to numbers.
structures.example: In my house we are six people, my mother, my father, my sister and my two brothers, plus my two cats, which are members of the family too. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; ; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'both … and' to combine noun phrases, to give emphasis.
structures.example: I felt sorry for you because both friends and family are very important and having to pick one is very hard. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Turkish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'BOTH … AND' WITH PHRASES AND CLAUSES
structures.can_do: Can use 'both … and' to combine phrases and clauses, often for emphasis.
structures.example: And we have won a high reputation both at home and abroad. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'neither … nor' to connect two words, phrases or clauses, often to give emphasis or focus.
structures.example: Neither you nor I would like that. (Sweden; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'Neither' or 'Nor' + inverted auxiliary or 'be' + subject to add to a previous related negative clause, to focus on an additional negative factor.
structures.example: Nevertheless, I have no recollection of ever leaving my diary. In fact, I can clearly remember that I kept it with me all the time I was working. Neither do I remember losing it during the time I was on the platform waiting for my train to pull in. (Spain; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'either … or' to combine more complex strings of clauses and sentences.
