structures.example: And finally, about the present, you have two options; either you get something typical from your country, which they may like because you know how much they like collecting things from all over the world, or I get something from the wedding list store and sent it to them with your name on it and we can sort it out when you arrive here. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1998; Catalan; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO' WITH INVERSION
structures.can_do: Can use inverted auxiliary 'do' + the subject after 'not only', to give focus.
structures.example: Indeed, not only did they teach us useful knowledge, but they also organised practical exercises to ensure that we had assimilated all the information. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use '(and) yet' to combine phrases and clauses to introduce a contrast, often unexpected.
structures.example: In the face of these recent events, our department also reviewed the contract with ProLine International, and found some interesting yet unpleasant details. (Romania; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Romanian; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use 'And yet' to combine sentences to introduce a contrast, often unexpected, sometimes in a formal context.
structures.example: If I had, I would try to do the best for them, just like my parents did, and very likely I would make the same mistakes. And yet, I think I would be a good and loving father. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'not only … but also' to combine phrases and clauses, often for focus or emphasis.
structures.example: This book is not only a guide to the history of music but also a compendium of theory. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'because' as a subordinating conjunction to introduce a subordinate clause.
structures.example: I want a big garden because I have children. (Arabic - Other)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of simple subordinating conjunctions ('as, after, before since, until, although, whether, so (that), though') to introduce a subordinate clause.
structures.example: In fact, I have to buy a desk, as I don't have one. (French)

structures.can_do: Can use more complex subordinating conjunctions ('as long as, as soon as, in order that, despite the fact that, due to the fact that, as if, as though') to introduce a subordinate clause.
structures.example: As far as I am concerned, keeping animals in zoos is not cruel as long as the zoos keep to certain rules concerning the conditions the animals have to be kept in. (Dutch)

structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of simple subordinating conjunctions ('once, whereas, unless, except (that) provided (that)'), to introduce a subordinate clause.
structures.example: Believe me, once you have tried it, you'll never give it up. (Spanish - Latin American)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of simple subordinating conjunctions '(if, when, so, while)' to introduce a subordinate clause.
structures.example: But if you don't take your car, you can rent a bike in the park too. (French)

structures.can_do: Can use 'whatever', 'wherever', 'however', etc. as a subordinating conjunction, at the beginning of a sentence, to give focus.
structures.example: Whatever you choose, you'll probably have to share it with other people. (Swedish)

structures.can_do: Can use 'in that' as a subordinating conjunction, to give greater in-depth explanation, often in formal contexts.
structures.example: Nowadays it is widely argued that professional sports are damaging to people's health in that they involve gruelling training sessions as an integral part of the occupation. (Russian)

structures.can_do: Can use articles 'the', 'a' and 'an' before nouns. ► noun phrases
structures.example: She lives in a small flat in the town - it's great! (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'a' + 'very' + adjectives in basic noun phrases. ► adverbs ►  noun phrases
structures.example: He's a very good man. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Mandarin; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'a' and 'an' before adjectives in a noun phrase. ► adjectives ►  noun phrases
structures.example: You can make a quick snack, for example a sandwich. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the' in prepositional phrases relating to time.
structures.example: I work at the weekend and I'm very busy from Monday to Friday. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2008; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use no article before a limited range of nouns in some fixed expressions with prepositions.
structures.example: If you are at home, I can come tomorrow. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Farsi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use no article before an increasing range of nouns in some fixed expressions with prepositions.
structures.example: The weather is very cold at night. (China; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'another' to talk about something additional.
structures.example: Dear Mary, I spent a week in Dubai and I am going to spend another week in Al Ain. (United Arab Emirates; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; Arabic - Gulf; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use no article before a limited range of singular, plural and uncountable nouns when referring to things in general.
structures.example: In my free time I usually play football. (Poland; A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2010; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the' + adjectives in a noun phrase, to specify.
structures.example: My house is opposite the new café. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use no article before an increasing range of singular and plural nouns when referring to things in general.
structures.example: Education in the future will change in a good way. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Tagalog; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can form a noun phrase with 'the' + superlative adjectives + noun.
structures.example: It has the latest technology. (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'another' with singular nouns. ► pronouns ► determiners
structures.example: Every 5 minutes, he makes another great joke. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2001; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'another' to talk about something different.
structures.example: I'm sorry but I won't be able to go to the English class tomorrow because I'll go to Maldonado to see my mother that is ill. But I can go another day to cover the work I've missed. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'the other' with a singular noun to refer to the second or the opposite of two things, and with a plural noun to refer to one of a set of things. ► pronouns ►  noun phrases
structures.example: She saw his blue jacket in a shop on the other side of the street. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' with uncountable nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I found this information in: www.artschool.com, (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the in comparative phrases 'more', 'less', 'worse', 'better … the more', 'less', 'worse …' to talk about one thing that is affected by another. ► comparative clauses
structures.example: [talking about how watching TV is bad for you] I mean that you can watch one or two hours a day but the more you watch, the worse you become. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' in a limited range of contexts to refer to places from the speaker's or writer's point of view. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I want to let you know about this area and the shops near here. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2008; ; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' with time and date words to refer to 'the one that's coming'.
structures.example: … this summer I want to spend my holiday in my country, Bulgaria. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2011; Bengali; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' with singular nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I like this place because is very nice and quiet. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'that' with singular nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I also want to see that film. (Myanmar; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; Burmese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'that' to talk about or point to things which are further away in time and space from the speaker or writer
structures.example: Placeholder row, lack of spoken data (see A2)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' to refer to something with immediate relevance which has already been mentioned. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: Could you send someone who can check where the problem is and try to do something about this problem. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' in an increasing range of contexts to refer to places and things from the speaker's or writer's point of view. ► noun phrases ► pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I am writing this letter to tell you about my favourite birthday present, which was a laptop. (United Arab Emirates; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Arabic - Gulf; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' in an increasing range of contexts to refer to places and things from the speaker's or writer's point of view. ► noun phrases ► pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I am writing this letter to tell you about my favourite birthday present which was a laptop. (United Arab Emirates; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Arabic - Gulf; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'these' with plural nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I bought these clothes because they weren't expensive. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'that' to refer to something which has already been mentioned. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: Yesterday, I went shopping to Collesione for clothes. I bought a skirt and a T-shirt, because we have a party this week. They were very cheap. They cost £10. You should go that shop. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'these' to refer to places and things from the speaker's or writer's point of view.
structures.example: Placeholder row, lack of spoken data (see A2)

structures.can_do: Can use 'those' to refer to things which have already been mentioned. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: I went shopping for clothes yesterday. I bought some jumpers and trousers. I bought those clothes because I'm going to Japan next Friday and there the weather is cold. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' with nouns and noun phrases in a narrative to create a sense of immediacy.
structures.example: [talking about two characters in a story] There's this flame of passion between them. (France; C2 MASTERY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' with time and date words to refer to the past.
structures.example: Hi Mark, Thank you for your lovely letter which I received this morning. (Libya; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Arabic - Meghreb; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'these' to refer to things with immediate relevance or which have already been mentioned. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: … you can visit the Old Museum, the Green Park, the old bridge and old church. These places are very old. (Libya; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2001; Arabic - Meghreb; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'those' to talk about or point to things which the speaker or writer perceives to be further away in time and space.
structures.example: Placeholder row, lack of spoken data (see A2)

structures.can_do: Can use 'this' + noun + 'of' + possessive pronoun to highlight something, often in a positive way.
structures.example: What is more, not only is this rare talent of theirs used for public pleasure but also for international sports success, which makes us all proud. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'those' with plural nouns. ► noun phrases ►  pronouns: demonstrative
structures.example: The cost of those clothes was £300. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use ''s' after singular or proper nouns to indicate possession.
structures.example: It's very important for me because it's my sister's jacket. (Uruguay; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use possessive determiners 'my', 'your', 'his', 'her' and 'our' before nouns. ► noun phrases ► possessive pronouns
structures.example: I live with my family. My home is a flat. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use quantifying determiners + possessive determiners + 'of' + noun. ► noun phrases
structures.example: All of my friends were there. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'that' and 'those' to convey emotional distance, often to express disapproval.
structures.example: I also told her that if I had been in her shoes, I would not have put up with that sort of behaviour. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use ''s' after a noun phrase with of to indicate possession.
structures.example: Actually, I know a great one and they can make a little discount for us because the owner is a friend of my father's . (Albania; B2 VANTAGE; 2009; Albanian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 's'' after plural nouns to indicate possession.
structures.example: I decided to spend the rest of my holiday in my parents' house, near the sea. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use ''s' after irregular plural nouns to indicate possession.
structures.example: When I go out with my friends, I actually like wearing clothes that attract people's attention. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'their' before nouns to refer to a generic body or group of people expressed as a singular subject. ► generic pronouns
structures.example: … yet everyone has their preference for one or another. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use possessive determiner 'their'. ► noun phrases ► possessive pronouns
structures.example: They were having the time of their lives, watching all the animals the zoo had, but when they returned to their car, they saw that someone was stealing Paul's suitcase. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use possessive determiner 'its' before nouns to refer to a singular inanimate subject or object.
structures.example: It was the biggest TV in the bazaar with its huge, black screen. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Turkish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: SINGULAR NOUN ENDING IN 'S' + APOSTROPHE
structures.can_do: Can use an apostrophe after singular nouns ending in 's', to indicate possession.
structures.example: However, I believe that in order to maintain its popularity, the programme should keep some of the series' aspects the same, but alter some others. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'one's' to indicate possession, referring to people in general.
structures.example: Living in Greece, I have had a chance to realise how much tourism can affect one's life. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of quantifying determiners with plural nouns ('some', 'lots of', 'a lot of' and numbers).
structures.example: Near my home there are some shops. (Portuguese, A1 BREAKTHROUGH, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use 'much' with uncountable nouns in negative contexts.
structures.example: But we didn't have much money, so we didn't buy many things. (Vietnam; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of quantifying determiners with singular nouns ('a', 'every').► determiners: articles
structures.example: In my home are 3 bedrooms. I have a big kitchen and small toilet. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of quantifying determiners with singular nouns ('each', 'an', 'one' and numbers).
structures.example: The new art class starts next Monday and each class is about 1 hour long. (Hong Kong; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Chinese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: WITH PLURAL AND UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS
structures.can_do: Can use a range of quantifying determiners ('some', 'any', 'no', 'more', 'a lot of') with both plural nouns and uncountable nouns.
structures.example: I think we should bring some water to drink. (Cyprus; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of quantifying determiners with plural nouns ('all', 'both', 'a few').
structures.example: This notice is for all students: we are going to have a concert at school. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use two possessive ''s' constructions in the same noun phrase.
structures.example: There were no photographs of him in Ann 's mother's albums. (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use ''s' without a following noun when the noun has already been mentioned or is obvious in the context.
structures.example: Olivia's experiences probably are the narrator's. (Italy; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'many' with plural nouns in negative contexts.
structures.example: There are n't many tickets. (other; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2010; Others; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'so many' and 'too many' with plural nouns.
structures.example: We played so many games, like dog and bone, four corners, and many more. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2004; Gujarati; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of quantifying determiners + 'of' + determiner ('half of', 'enough of', 'none of',).► pronouns
structures.example: In my opinion you should spend half of your holiday with your parents and the other half with your friends: I think this would be the best thing to do. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM: WITH PLURAL AND UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS
structures.can_do: Can use an increasing range of quantifying determiners with both plural nouns and uncountable nouns ('most', 'enough', 'plenty of', 'loads of').
structures.example: I'm convinced that most people watch too much TV these days. (Russian, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2010)

structures.guideword: FORM: 'SO MUCH', 'TOO MUCH' WITH UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS
structures.can_do: Can use 'so much' and 'too much' with uncountable nouns.
structures.example: Hello Marina. Unfortunately I have so much work at the moment that I can't help you. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2005; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'much' with uncountable nouns in interrogative contexts.
Can use quantifying determiners with uncountable nouns, often in informal and/or spoken contexts ('a little', 'a bit of' and 'a little bit of').
structures.example: I went with my friends so we could spend a little time together. (Spanish - Latin American, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2003)

structures.can_do: Can use 'many' with plural nouns in interrogative contexts.
structures.example: Have you got many friends in England? (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of quantifying determiners + 'of' + determiner ('all of', 'some of', 'both of', 'many of', 'any of', number + 'of', 'each of'). ► pronouns: quantity
structures.example: I spent all of my money! (Turkish, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of quantifying determiners with plural nouns ('several', 'millions of', 'a few of').
structures.example: So several days ago we received a complaint. (Chinese, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2002)

structures.can_do: Can use 'either' and 'neither' + 'of' with plural noun phrases or pronouns.► pronouns
structures.example: Either of the measures is recommended and those measures are bound to enhance the company's competitive power. (China; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2002; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use determiners in hyperbole, often in informal contexts ('millions of', 'loads of', 'tons of').
structures.example: My kitchen is absolutely cramped. I love cooking and despite the fact that I have no space, I managed to fit in a table as well as millions of cookbooks and all the necessary kitchen tools. (German, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 2000)

structures.can_do: Can use 'either' and 'neither' with singular nouns.
structures.example: Second, we would draw your attention to the fact that neither party could foresee or predict the recent rise in the price of wheat. (Russia; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use modifier + 'little' + uncountable nouns and modifier + 'few' + countable nouns, to indicate a lack of something or not as much as expected of something.► adverbs
structures.example: I spend very little time outside, and I know I do not have enough stamina and strength. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can modify determiners with adverbs. ► adverbs
structures.example: Because almost all of the programmes are stupid. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Turkish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'MANY A' WITH SINGULAR NOUNS, FOR FOCUS
structures.can_do: Can use 'many a' or 'many an' + singular noun for emphasis and focus.
structures.example: We have come a long way and climbed many a mountain but are we really better off than our ancestors? (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'AS YOU KNOW', ORGANISING, MARKING SHARED KNOWLEDGE
structures.can_do: Can use 'as you know' as a discourse marker of shared knowledge.
structures.example: I can't come to your wedding because, as you know, I live in England and on Thursday 18th July I'm going to take the FCE exam. (A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of words and phrases as discourse markers to add information.
structures.example: Moreover the health of our staff and customers is essential. (Switzerland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; German; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: ORGANISING, MARKING NEW KNOWLEDGE, INFORMAL
structures.can_do: Can use 'you see', 'the thing is' as discourse markers to mark new knowledge, usually in informal contexts.
structures.example: You see, in the park, you can enjoy fresh air… (Vietnam; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'so' as a discourse marker to summarise, usually in informal contexts.
structures.example: So, what do you think? (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use sequencing adverbs as discourse markers to organise text.
structures.example: Firstly, we need a good expert to run the course. Secondly, good materials are needed. (China; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to introduce contrasting statements.
structures.example: On the one hand going to a large school is better for making friends, but on the other hand I think you can learn better in a small school. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to introduce a comparison.
structures.example: [talking about celebrating New Year] But some countries celebrate on other dates too, like they have Chinese New Year according to their calendar.  Likewise, in Nepal New Year is celebrated on 1st of Baishak, which is the start of a new year according to the Nepalese calendar. (B2 VANTAGE; 2011; Breton; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to summarise.
structures.example: Thus, I would be very grateful if you would send me clear explanations of the following points: firstly, I would like you to specify what “the normal price” is, and therefore what would be the cost of two nights. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs as discourse markers to indicate an attitude or viewpoint.
structures.example: Unfortunately, they filmed only the building and the garden, not the students! (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to point to other parts of a text.
structures.example: As mentioned above, it might be possible to negotiate better contracts for your company. (Switzerland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Swiss German; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: ORGANISING, OPENINGS AND CLOSINGS, FORMAL
structures.can_do: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to open and close texts and point to conclusions, often in formal contexts.
structures.example: To begin with, I want to ensure that you are going to have a great time with us. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use adverbs in the front position for focus.
structures.example: That's my diary, the dearest thing I had. Here I wrote how I felt, what I did, who I met and all my problems. (Italy; B1 THRESHOLD; 2000; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + 'be' + adjective + 'that-'clause for focus.
structures.example: It's great that you have got a new job! (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use prepositional phrases in the front position for focus.
structures.example: In the morning, I go to the beach. (Argentina; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'THE THING/ FACT/ POINT/ PROBLEM IS (THAT)'
structures.can_do: Can use 'The thing, fact, point, problem, or reason + is (that)' for focus.
structures.example: The reason is I like children, I have experience of looking after disabled people and I like to do things like volunteering. (B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Japanese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'The reason (that)', 'The place (which)' + clause as subject + 'be' for focus. ► Relative clauses
structures.example: The reason I am writing is to suggest a few things about our holidays. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use fixed expressions in the front position for focus.
structures.example: At the end of the day everything is up to you! (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2000; Greek; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use 'Not a' + noun with a passive verb or inverted auxiliary and subject for focus.
structures.example: Not a word was spoken by anyone throughout the journey. (Cyprus; C2 MASTERY; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'What' + noun or pronoun + verb phrase as subject + 'be', for focus.
structures.example: What we need is a strong publicity campaign, directed at young people. (Portugal; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use imperatives as pointing devices within texts for focus.
structures.example: Note the disadvantages of this transfer. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2002; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'Wh-'cleft clauses as titles or subtitles, to point to something that follows, for focus.
structures.example: Why I think this is a good idea

structures.can_do: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with an '-ed' form, before a main clause, for focus, often in formal, academic or business contexts.
structures.example: Compared to other European capitals, there has been a lot done to make riding a bike less dangerous and more comfortable in Berlin. (Germany; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1998; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'The' + premodifier + 'thing, fact, point, problem or reason' + 'is (that)' for focus.
structures.example: The sad thing about it was that it was actually Richard who said, "Why don't you go on holiday?” (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'How', 'Why', or 'Where' cleft clauses as subject, for focus
structures.example: How we are brought up forms our character, our thinking and our attitude towards ourselves and towards everybody and everything around us. (Switzerland; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use 'It' + 'be' + noun + 'that' clause for focus.
structures.example: It is Lily who decides to go to the seaside and it is also her who kills the turkey given by a lorry-driver. (France; C2 MASTERY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use more than one fixed expression in the front position for added focus.
structures.example: But all of a sudden, out of nowhere a bunch of people came running towards him, yelling something he couldn't understand. (Switzerland; C2 MASTERY; 2000; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form with 'will'.
structures.example: I'll be waiting for you. (Portugal; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form with 'will' and 'shall'.
structures.example: However, I shall be attending class the day after tomorrow and I shall cover the work I miss by copying it from John. (India; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Tamil; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future continuous with 'will' to talk about an event or action in progress at a specified time in the future.
structures.example: Tomorrow please come at 4.30 pm because I'll be working before. (France; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form with 'will' ('won’t').
structures.example: I would like you to know that I won't be attending your English class next week. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future continuous with 'will' as a polite question form, in place of the present simple or future simple.
structures.example: Will I be needing any money? (Switzerland; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future continuous with 'might' or 'may' to talk about an event or activity potentially in progress at a specified or understood time in the future.
structures.example: As far as I'm concerned, we should definitely do some additional publicity, particularly for the new offerings which might be coming up. (Netherlands; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'yes/no' and 'wh-' question forms with 'will'.
structures.example: Will they be holding any activities at night? (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present forms of 'be' + 'about to'.
structures.example: You are not going to believe what I am about to tell you! (Chile; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'going to' to talk about the future from a point in the past. ► 'be going to'
structures.example: She was going to return it but she saw something very strange, her number was on the screen. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be due to' and, more formally, 'be to' talk about things that are scheduled or expected.
structures.example: Our annual conference for HR managers is due to take place on 10 December 2010. (Austria; B2 VANTAGE; 2010; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present form of 'be' + 'to'.
structures.example: Dear Erica, I am sorry that I cannot attend the meeting at head office as expected, as I am to go on a business trip to New York then. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2002; Chinese; Pass)

structures.guideword: USE: OBLIGATIONS AND  INSTRUCTIONS WITH 'BE TO'
structures.can_do: Can use 'be to' talk about future obligations and to give instructions.
structures.example: [talking about gorillas] We have no right to do so, because they are to be respected as much as any other living form on this planet! (Italy; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Italian; Pass)

structures.guideword: USE: IMMEDIATE FUTURE WITH 'BE ABOUT TO'
structures.can_do: Can use 'be about to' to talk about the immediate future, often with 'just'.
structures.example: I know what you 're about to answer, and moreover you might be right; (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present form of 'be' + 'due to'.
structures.example: I am afraid that July is the only appropriate month, because I am due to start work in August. (Turkey; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'would' to talk about the future from a point in the past.► 'would'
structures.example: I've just bought a new dress, and a beautiful black T-shirt. When I saw them, I thought they would be great for tonight's party. (Spanish - Latin American, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2010)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form with 'will'.
structures.example: This summer I will have been working for three years for my company … (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'on the point of' + '-ing' to talk about things that were expected to happen soon after a point in the past.
structures.example: In addition, when I was on the point of leaving the office, another phone rang. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2002; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'about to' (often with 'just') to talk about the immediate future from a point in the past.
structures.example: Two days before, I told him that our father was about to buy a brand new car. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'due to' to talk about scheduled events in the future from a point in the past.
structures.example: It was quite early in the morning, only 7.15 am, and my plane was due to leave in about 40 minutes. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect continuous to make assumptions about the present.
structures.example: I do not think that this aspect is really necessary because it is supposed that … you will have been studying very hard to occupy that job …. (Argentina; C2 MASTERY; 2005; Spanish - Latin American; Fail)

structures.guideword: USE: LOOKING BACK FROM A POINT IN THE FUTURE
structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect continuous to look back to the past from a point in the future and to emphasise the duration of an activity or event.
structures.example: Now I am staying in Hastings in England and this month, I will have been studying English for seven months. (Korea, South; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; Korean; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form with 'will'.
structures.example: I'm sure I will have learned today's lesson by the next lesson. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 2003; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form with 'will'.
structures.example: I think that the best time for me to visit Scotland would be in July, because I will not have finished my university exams by June. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.guideword: USE: EVENTS COMPLETED IN THE FUTURE
structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' to talk about something which is expected to be completed (or not completed) by a certain point in the future.
structures.example: There is no problem if you want to leave at 4.30 pm as the match will have finished by that time. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect with adverbs (in the normal mid-position).
structures.example: If you have ever read a fairytale by Hans Christian Andersen you will surely have discovered why this man is so famous worldwide. (Denmark; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2001; Danish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form of the future perfect simple.
structures.example: Will he have changed? (Spain; C2 MASTERY; 1998; Catalan; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' to make assumptions about the present, particularly with 'you'.
structures.example: As you will have heard, this year's work experience programme in Britain was in general a success. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' as a politeness strategy, often in formal contexts.
structures.example: [from a formal letter] I hope I will have reassured you. (France; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative forms 'will' and ''ll'.
structures.example: I will see you soon. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Urdu; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' and ''ll' to talk about plans and intentions.
structures.example: I will try to come to see you tomorrow. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Romanian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms 'will not' and 'won't'.
structures.example: Without them I will not be able to play football. (Spain; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question forms of 'will' and 'shall'.
structures.example: Will you come? (Russia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form 'shall' with 'I' and 'we'.
structures.example: I shall come with you. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; Hindi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall I' to make offers.
structures.example: Shall I wait for you? (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' to make requests.
structures.example: Will you come tomorrow at 6.35 pm to my house? (Italy; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' to ask about plans and intentions.
structures.example: Will you have a mobile phone? (France; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall we' to make suggestions.
structures.example: Shall we go to my friend's house to get it? (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2005; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall' with 'I' and 'we' to talk about plans and intentions.
structures.example: I promise that I shall cover all the work and give it to you tomorrow. (Thai, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2006)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' and '‘ll' to make predictions.
structures.example: It will be hotter because of global warming.  (2246945_2; PET; Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form 'shall not'.
structures.example: However, we shall not forget to mention the legal and social consequences of such a merger to the average employees. (Switzerland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Swiss German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall' to talk about long-term intentions.
structures.example: I must believe, believe in myself and in everybody else, and mainly in what I look for, this way I shall never lose hope. (Mexico; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' to talk about fixed plans, often with timetabled times and dates.
structures.example: The work will start at 8 a.m. and finish at 2 p.m. The new schedule starts on 1 June. (Russia; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' to express willingness.
structures.example: My mother will drive us there. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Malay; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative and question forms of 'be going to' talk about plans and intentions.
structures.example: I'm going to use pink paint. (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2006; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form.
structures.example: What are you going to wear? (Italy; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall' to make predictions, usually in formal contexts.
structures.example: Once more I invite you wholeheartedly to stay at my place and I hope we shall meet in November. (Poland; C2 MASTERY; 1998; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: [about some new jeans] I 'm going to wear them on holiday. (Turkey; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form.
structures.example: I am not going to go to school tomorrow. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the past form of 'be' + 'going to'. ► future in the past
structures.example: When we realized it was going to be an extremely hot day, we took water. (Argentina; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'going to' with a limited range of adverbs, after the auxiliary be form, in the normal mid position.
structures.example: I know that I 'm never going to forget this moment. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form of 'be going to' to talk about plans and intentions.
structures.example: I 'm not going to be able to meet you next Tuesday, because I have to go to the dentist at 5.30. (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the past form of 'be going to' to refer to the future from a point in the past. ► future in the past
structures.example: She didn't know what was going to happen. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be going to' with 'be' to make predictions.
structures.example: I think this Saturday is going to be a nice day. (Mexico; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2003; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the past form of 'be going to' as the reported form.► reported speech
structures.example: Fortunately, he was told his boss was going to be a bit late, so he had some time to go back home. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be going to' with an increasing range of verbs to make predictions.
structures.example: I think you're going to like it. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'going to' with an increasing range of adverbs (particularly adverbs of certainty) in the normal mid position.
structures.example: Mario Soares is already an old man, nearly 70, who is probably going to finish his active political life in 2 or 3 years. (Portugal; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'going to' with a wide range of adverbs before the main verb.
structures.example: But I don't know if I'm going to still live here. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the past form of 'be going to' (often followed by 'but') to talk about a plan, sometimes one that may have changed.
structures.example: We were going to get married two months ago but we broke up and I really didn't know why. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with a limited range of verbs to talk about future arrangements.
structures.example: I'm working this Saturday and Sunday morning. (Spanish - European, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with a limited range of verbs to ask about future plans.
structures.example: [talking about a Rolling Stones concert] Are you coming? (Swiss German, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2010)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with an increasing range of verbs to talk about future arrangements.
structures.example: I’m attending my grandmother’s funeral tomorrow. (B1 Malay)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with an increasing range of verbs to ask about future plans.
structures.example: Are you visiting my country on your next holiday? (B1 Korean)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of verbs to talk about future arrangements.
structures.example: We’re throwing a party for fun on 5th January. (B2 French)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple with 'when' to refer to the future.
structures.example: I'll tell you more when I meet you. (Vietnam; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Vietnamese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple to talk about timetabled events in the future.
structures.example: [Talking about a film] It begins on 8 o'clock in the evening. (Switzerland; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2009; Swiss German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple with 'I hope' to talk about hopes and wishes for the future.
structures.example: I hope you enjoy your holiday too. (A2, Chinese)

structures.can_do: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of common verbs to ask about future plans.
structures.example: So are you planning to visit Japan then? (B2 Japan)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple with 'as soon as' to refer to the future.
structures.example: I'm planning to move as soon as I finish college because job opportunities in my area aren't good. (B1 Portuguese)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple with 'by the time' to refer to the future.
structures.example: … by the time he gets home, he will just want to go straight to bed. (C1 Spanish - Latin American)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple after speech act verbs expressing suggestions and obligation.
structures.example: We would suggest that our management takes a closer look. (C1 German)

structures.can_do: Can use the present simple with 'only when' (followed by 'will' and inverted subject) to refer to the future.
structures.example: Only when we understand that, will we be able to live in better societies. (C2 Spanish - Latin American)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + 'be' + 'important' + ('that') clause.
structures.example: It's important that you take breaks and don't work all the time. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'if-' clauses + 'possible', as a politeness strategy.
structures.example: If it is possible I would like to pay by credit card. (B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; ; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + 'be' + adjective + 'to' + infinitive, to make an assertion more or less direct.
structures.example: Our sales department staff are heavily involved in several international projects, so it is necessary to improve their foreign language skills. (Germany; B1 THRESHOLD; 2006; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'I' + 'be' + 'sure' + clause.
structures.example: I'm sure I can beat you at chess. (Malaysia; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2007; Malay; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + 'be' + adjective + 'for' + object + 'to' + infinitive.
structures.example: If you have to choose between two schools, I think it's important for you to know what they’re like. (Peru; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause.
structures.example: It seems clear to me that swimming is good for the whole body. (B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IT' + LINKING VERB + ADJECTIVES + CLAUSE, HEDGING
structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause to make an assertion less direct.
structures.example: It does not seem possible that we can live without any private life. (Japan; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Japanese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: 'IT' + LINKING VERB + ADJECTIVES + ('THAT') CLAUSE, FOCUS
structures.can_do: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause as a focusing device.
structures.example: It is clear that we can't live without computers today. (Russia; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use pronoun or noun + 'be' + adjective + 'to' + (past) infinitive.
structures.example: They are unlikely to arrive on Friday. (India; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Hindi; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: You can see a lot of special places in Wroclaw. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2007, Polish)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative question form.
structures.example: Can you come for dinner Monday at 6.00 pm? (Arabic - Other, A1 BREAKTHROUGH, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms.
structures.example: I cannot come to see you. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2009, Bengali)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to make an offer.
structures.example: Can I help you? (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2009, Lithuanian)

structures.can_do: Can modify adjectives with adverbs, often for emphasis.
structures.example: It is painfully obvious that it will rescue our city from the pollution and fumes that cars are producing. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Polish; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to talk about ability to do something.
structures.example: I can cook. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2009, Turkish)

structures.can_do: Can modify adjectives with degree adverbs, often to make an assertion less direct.
structures.example: If you want to come earlier or if there's a public transport strike (which is quite probable), you will have to take a taxi. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to give and refuse permission or talk about what is forbidden.
structures.example: You can wear anything you want. (A2 WAYSTAGE, 2008, Spanish - Latin American)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to make a request.
structures.example: Can you come on Sunday at seven o’clock? (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2010, Arabic)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to talk about possibility.
structures.example: The shop is next to the post office. There you can find milk, juices and sweets but you can't buy meat. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH, 2008, Spanish - Other)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative question forms in main clauses and question tags.
structures.example: Can't you go with your parents some time and with your friends later? (Spain; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' with a limited range of adverbs (including 'also', 'always', 'even', 'just', 'only', 'really', 'still') in the normal mid position after the modal verb.   ► adverbs
structures.example: You can also write postcards and letters to your friends. (B1 THRESHOLD, 2008, German)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can be' to talk about general truths and tendencies.
structures.example: … spending an entire summer without your friends can be very boring. (B1 THRESHOLD, 2008,  Spanish - European)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can you believe' to express surprise.
structures.example: They invented a robot which plays football, can you believe this? (B1 THRESHOLD, 2008, Portuguese)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' with an increasing range of adverbs (including 'easily', 'hardly', 'now', 'probably', 'sometimes', 'still') in the normal mid position after the modal verb or after the subject in questions.  ► adverbs
structures.example: In case you need them , I can easily provide references. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1998; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' to talk about general truths and tendencies.
structures.example: …some young people can feel bored when they have to walk a lot and look at […] very old things. (Polish, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 1999)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms of 'can't' and 'cannot' to guess, predict and deduce.
structures.example: You look very pale and you can’t be feeling well. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a wide range of adverbs with 'can' in the normal mid position after the modal verb). ► adverbs
structures.example: Only those who live with their relatives can fully understand how essential is the role of your parents, sisters, aunts... (Yugoslavia; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Serbian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use negative forms of 'can' to make reproaches or appeals.
structures.example: You can’t forget your friends. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'how can' to reflect, through rhetorical questions.
structures.example: And how can we improve if we are not allowed to make mistakes, evaluate our experiences in a new light and try again? (Netherlands; C2 MASTERY; 1998; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use expressions with 'can' or 'can’t' to give focus or add emphasis, such as 'as you can see', 'I can't say', 'I can tell you that', 'as you can imagine', 'I can say that', 'I can assure you that'.
structures.example: So, as you can see, there are no serious consequences for us, so far. (C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can' in passive reporting clauses in a more formal impersonal style (e.g. for reports and academic contexts), such as 'It can be said that', 'It can be argued (that)', 'It can be concluded that', 'It can be considered'.► passives
structures.example: It can be argued, looking at the figures, that the company should consider withdrawing from the heater market. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2003; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'can't' or 'cannot have' + '-ed' to make deductions.
structures.example: I live with my partner and we can't have used so much electricity. (C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2009; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use negative form dare not and daren't +  infinitive without to.
structures.example: [talking about a restaurant] But many local people dare not go to Lily, because it is too expensive. (Taiwan; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use affirmative form dare + infinitive without to.
structures.example: I can cook if you dare eat it! (Taiwan; B2 VANTAGE; 2001; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use semi-modal 'dare' to talk about being brave enough to do something.
structures.example: Some people object that I have to put up with the rain and other inconveniences, but I think that they are rather jealous because they daren't give up their car. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the fixed expression 'I dare say' to say that something is probably true.
structures.example: I feel that I have a huge responsibility trying to choose only one option, but I dare say that the last option may be the best one. (Argentina; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'will' + 'be able to' + infinitive to talk about possibility and ability.
structures.example: Will you be able to come this time? (Brazil; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form.
structures.example: Dare we run the risk of even one child or adult turning to violent crime because they think it is ok? (Greece; 2010; English)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of modal verbs + 'be able to' + infinitive.
structures.example: After finishing school, you might be able to hang out with your friends. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be allowed to' to talk about permission.
structures.example: My mother went with me on this trip because I wasn't allowed to go by myself. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form 'didn't dare' + infinitive without 'to' to talk about not being brave enough to do something.
structures.example: She didn't dare think about him and the possibility that he would never come back. (Sweden; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'how dare … !' to express disapproval or offense about something
structures.example: How dare people say that we don't practice sport! (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Catalan; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a limited range of expressions with 'be' + infinitive ('be allowed to', 'be supposed to', 'be able to') with present and past forms of 'be' and with modal 'will'.
structures.example: First of all, if you are allowed to go out of the building in your break, you should do it. (Cyprus; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'was supposed to', 'were supposed to' to refer to past or future arrangements which may not have happened or may change.
structures.example: I am really sorry, but I will have to make some changes to my trip. I was supposed to arrive on 11th June 2003, but I will arrive the next month. (Mexico; B1 THRESHOLD; 2003; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the full range of expressions with 'be' + infinitive ('be likely to', 'be due to', 'be meant to', 'be bound to', 'be sure to', 'be certain to', 'be obliged to') with present and past forms of 'be' and with modal 'will' .
structures.example: People who read books are likely to be more knowledgeable. (Argentina; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'was able to', 'were able to' to talk about facts in the past.
structures.example: [about a bus journey] She was able to get a good seat and she unexpectedly got to school early. (Philippines; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Tagalog; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be meant to' to talk about ideal states.
structures.example: Animals are meant to be free, and man should be very careful about interfering with nature. (Swedish, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 1993)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be due to' and, more formally, 'be to' to talk about things that are scheduled or expected.
structures.example: I have attached the … company law directive enacted 2 years ago and which is due to be implemented by 2008. (Austria; B2 VANTAGE; 2007; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' (+modifier) 'likely to' to talk about probability.
structures.example: And whenever money is involved, some problems are likely to happen. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use '(much) more/less' to modify 'likely' in a comparison.
structures.example: In case of an accident, one is more likely to be badly injured when riding a bicycle. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be supposed to' to talk about hearsay or supposition.
structures.example: That woman is supposed to have killed her husbands (at least two), because she wanted their money. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' (+ modifier) 'bound to' to talk about something certain or inevitable.
structures.example: I assure you that it is bound to be popular with different clients, especially young people and white-collar workers. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 2008; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'obvious/sure/likely/certain' followed by a 'that'-clause.
structures.example: It is about 1000 years old, so I am sure that you will find it fascinating to see it. (Japan; B2 VANTAGE; 2001; Japanese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be supposed to' to talk about expectation or obligation.
structures.example: However, the show is only on the 14th of March, the same day we are supposed to go to a Science Museum. (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the imperative form 'be sure to', to express obligation.
structures.example: If you cannot attend, be sure to inform me in advance. (Chinese, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be sure to', 'be certain to' to talk about certainty.
structures.example: A person that will act in that way is sure to be successful. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2009; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be forced to' to talk about an unnamed obligation, where the circumstances are beyond the control of the speaker/writer.
structures.example: I don't like to be forced to do something that I don't want to do. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'not' + adjective + 'that-' clause to make an assertion less direct.
structures.example: [talking about a town near a dump where people cannot open their windows] I am not certain that they have got used to it. (France; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be set to' to talk about strong assertion about the future, especially in institutional contexts.
structures.example: The turnover of our company is set to increase dramatically after the establishment of the e-shop, which itself requires little investment. (China; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2002; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + 'not' + adjective + 'to' + infinitive.
structures.example: The country's population is not likely to increase fast enough. (France; C2 MASTERY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be obliged to' to talk about an external obligation, especially in institutional contexts.
structures.example: The Sales Representatives are obliged to participate. (Switzerland; B2 VANTAGE; 2005; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question forms.
structures.example: What do you have to wear? (Thai, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2006)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms.
structures.example: You don't have to bring many things with you. (Greek, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2006)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative forms.
structures.example: This weekend I have to go to a party. (Hungarian, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use 'have (got) to' to talk about obligations.
structures.example: The concert starts at midnight but we have to go before then because we have got to buy our tickets. (Spanish - European, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2010)

structures.can_do: Can use 'be' + adjective + 'not' + 'to' + infinitive for emphasis.
structures.example: People should be obliged not to have more than a very small number of children otherwise they will be punished. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use present and past forms of 'have to' + '-ed' to talk about obligations in the past.
structures.example: Nowadays, one has to have finished at least senior high school for any employer to consider hiring you. (Greek, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 2005)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: [talking about clothes] So I may need them. (India; A2 WAYSTAGE; 2008; Gujarati; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use a range of present and past forms of 'have (got) to' to talk about deductions and conclusions.  ► must  ► had to
structures.example: [talking about a castle on a small island] It's got to be incredible to see a castle emerging from the sea. (Spanish - European, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 2001)

structures.can_do: Can use the fixed expression 'I have to admit' for emphasis.
structures.example: I have to admit that I watch a lot of TV, specially movies and soap operas, I love them. (Spanish - Latin American, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2010)

structures.can_do: Can use 'have to' as an infinitive form.
structures.example: I am going to have to buy new curtains. (Spanish - Latin American, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2001)

structures.can_do: Can use 'have to have' + '-ed'.
structures.example: [talking about urban versus rural life] In order to have an objective view on which lifestyle tends to be more problematic, you certainly have to have lived at each setting for a rather extensive time period. (Greek, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 2001)

structures.can_do: Can use 'you (have) got to' to make a strong suggestion.
structures.example: If you think you have seen almost everything in this world, you've got to see this museum. (Spanish - European, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 1998)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may' to talk about weak possibility referring to the present and the future.
structures.example: [talking about an important document] It may be in our room inside my bag. (Assamese, A2 WAYSTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may' with a limited range of adverbs (most commonly 'also') in the normal mid-position after the modal verb. ► adverbs
structures.example: I may also ask you for another favour.... (India; B1 THRESHOLD; 2005; Hindi; Fail)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form.
structures.example: I knew I may not meet him again. (Thailand; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Thai; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form with 'I'.
structures.example: May I give you a short presentation on 17th December? (China; B1 THRESHOLD; 2002; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may I' to ask for permission.
structures.example: May I be your guide while you stay here? (Brazil; B1 THRESHOLD; 2004; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may' with an increasing range of adverbs (most commonly 'even', 'only', 'already', 'never', 'just', 'sometimes') in the normal mid-position after the modal verb. ► adverbs
structures.example: When you're reading books, you may even find words you don't know and if you're an interested person, you will try to find out what it means, thus improving your vocabulary. (Portugal; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may not have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility in the past.
structures.example: The percentage of Dutch people eating a big, hot breakfast may not have been as high as of English people, but it has certainly reduced. (Netherlands; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1998; Dutch; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may I' to make a polite request, command or suggestion in formal contexts.
structures.example: May I have your attention please? (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility in the past.
structures.example: I think that he may have forgiven me for that accident … ! (Italy; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Italian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may I' to make a polite request for permission.
structures.example: Sir, may I come in? (Taiwan; B2 VANTAGE; 2001; Thai; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may well' to give emphasis to something unexpected.
structures.example: I think they may well come to an agreement on these payment problems. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may' in phrases such as as 'you may know', or 'as you may have' + '-ed' to focus the reader on shared knowledge.
structures.example: I usually take more than one book because, as you may know, it takes many hours to get there. (Spain; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may … but' to express an unexpected point of view.
structures.example: This may surprise you but I've managed to lose some weight, which I'm proud of. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 2003; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may as well' to talk about what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative or when it will not spoil the situation if you do that thing. ► might
structures.example: A few minutes later, she began hesitantly: "After all, you may as well know…” (France; C2 MASTERY; 1993; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'it may be' + '-ed' that as a hedging device when drawing conclusions and summarising, particularly in academic contexts.
structures.example: On balance, it may be concluded that although international sports competitions do involve such factors as serious and physical strain and commercial gain, their ultimate aim remains unchanged - namely, to find out in a fair way who deserves the title of the winner. (Russia; C2 MASTERY; 2003; Russian; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'may' in a subordinate clause expressing concession with 'however', 'whatever', 'whoever' … + 'it or this may be or seem'.
structures.example: But honestly, I am sure that the price of the watch also contributes its part, however small it may be, to my love of it. (Switzerland; C2 MASTERY; 2000; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: The weather might be hot and sunny. (Spanish - Latin American, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might' to make polite suggestions and give advice.
structures.example: The park is a great place for picnic. It has lots of trees, a beautiful view and fresh air. You might need to bring some food and drink. (Turkish, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility with a past reference.
structures.example: Many things might have led to these changes. (B2 VANTAGE; 2007; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might have' + '-ed'.
structures.example: [talking about an unusual sound] It might have been our neighbours' cat. (Swedish, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 1993)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might' as the past form of 'may' in indirect reports.
structures.example: … my parents said it might be the last holiday where we are all together. (German, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might' to talk about weak possibility.
structures.example: My dad isn’t working that day, he might take us. (Swahili, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form.
structures.example: I like to wear a shirt and pants. It might not be very fashionable, it might look simple, but that's the way I like it. (Thai, B1 THRESHOLD, Pass, 2006)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might not have' + '-ed'.
structures.example: First of all, not 45 but only 35 stalls were promised, meaning the disappointment you mentioned might not have been as bad as you, or whoever gave you the information, thought it was. (Argentina; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2000; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might not have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility with a past reference.
structures.example: The survey, mentioned in the local newspaper yesterday, might not have asked an accurate sample of people. (Brazil; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might' in phrases, such as 'as you might know', 'have already heard', to focus the reader on shared knowledge.
structures.example: As you might know, nobody came here until Wednesday afternoon. (Spanish - European, B2 VANTAGE, Pass, 2010)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form.
structures.example: Could it be possible that your company sent me the wrong bill, or might it be the bill from the last person who lived in my house? (German, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms.
structures.example: … you mustn't forget to buy some strawberry juice for us. (Portuguese, A2 WAYSTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form to make polite criticisms and suggestions.
structures.example: Last but not least, might it not be wise if you had more trips …? (Greek, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 2008)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might' followed by 'but' to console or justify.
structures.example: The argument that fashion reflects people's attitudes and behaviour might sound superficial, but on closer examination it turns out to be true. (Swiss German, C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY, Pass, 2004)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: You must wear your sports shoes and you must also bring your racket! (Greek)

structures.can_do: Can use 'try as I might' for emphasis at the beginning of a sentence.
structures.example: Try as I might, I was never able to persuade her to go for a walk. (Greek, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 1993)

structures.can_do: Can use 'might as well', mostly to talk about or suggest what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative. ► 'may'
structures.example: Living longer allows you to fulfil the different stages of your personal development, and if you reach the necessary maturity and integrity that corresponds to this stage of your life, you might as well make the best of these years. (Catalan, C2 MASTERY, Pass, 1993)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' to make invitations.
structures.example: You must come and stay in our house too. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2007; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' with a limited range of adverbs (most commonly 'also') in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs
structures.example: I must also do the FCE practice test because I will have the FCE test soon. (Chinese, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' with a limited range of pronouns ('I' and 'you') to talk about obligation and necessity.
structures.example: [talking about a mobile phone] It is very important to me because I must call my parents. (Spanish - Latin American, A2 WAYSTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use ellipted 'must' without a subject. ► ellipsis
structures.example: [at the end of a letter] Must go now. (Uruguay; B1 THRESHOLD; 2009; Spanish - Latin American; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' with the following verb ellipted where the previous main verb is understood.    ► ellipsis
structures.example: You must! It's amazing! (Italian, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' to guess and deduce, most commonly with 'it must be', or 'you must be'.
structures.example: Second, it must be boring for you to sit at a computer all day. (Turkish, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form.
structures.example: Is it possible to use the prize next year or must I cancel my trip to India? (Swedish, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' (with a wide range of pronouns and nouns) to talk about obligation and necessity.
structures.example: [talking about something the speaker has found] She took it and said we must go and find him. (Poland; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Polish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' to make strong, encouraging suggestions.
structures.example: This club has been opened for just two weeks. I mean we must see it. (Czech, B1 THRESHOLD)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must have' + '-ed'.
structures.example: When I realized that he must have forgotten, I called him up. (Chinese, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use the fixed expression 'I must say' to give emphasis, usually about something positive.
structures.example: I must say that I'm most delighted to have you here with us, Mr. Saramago, and it's with enormous pleasure that my students will hear your words. (Portuguese, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' with an increasing range of adverbs (including 'all', 'never', 'strongly', 'first') in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs
structures.example: To sum up, we must all act immediately because the existence of humanity may be in danger. (Greek, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use ellipted 'must have' + '-ed' without a subject. ► ellipsis
structures.example: [from a story] 'Must have fallen out of a car, or somfin'" This was his next thought. (Polish, C2 MASTERY)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' to ask about obligation and necessity.
structures.example: Is it possible to use the prize next year or must I cancel my trip to India? (Swedish, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use the perfect form of 'must' to make deductions about the past.
structures.example: Of course, India must have changed a lot since Jules Verne wrote his book, but I think that its charm remains. (French, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use the fixed expression 'I must admit' or 'you must admit' to express concession.
structures.example: On the other hand you must admit that not all ready-made meals taste really good and often they are not as healthy as fresh ones. (German, B2 VANTAGE)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative forms of 'must' to talk about what is not permitted.
structures.example: You must not hit them or punish them without good reason if you do not want them to become your worst enemy. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must not have been' (especially with 'easy').
structures.example: But I would like to stress that I was really happy that she found another husband, although she had three little children which must not have been easy for him. (German, C2 MASTERY)

structures.can_do: Can use 'must' with a wide range of adverbs in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs|
structures.example: There must certainly be other solutions to the problem of the need for space for new houses. (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2008; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can invert 'must' and the subject after negative phrases, e.g. 'not only', 'never', 'nor', to change the focus and give prominence/emphasis.
structures.example: Not only must you study really hard during university, but also keep studying afterwards. (Portuguese, C2 MASTERY)

structures.can_do: Can use 'needn't have' + '-ed'.
structures.example: You needn't have bought me anything! (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Spanish - European; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: I think you ought to go on holiday with both of them. (Turkey; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; Turkish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'ought to' with 'you' to give advice.
structures.example: Then, if you'd rather go with your friend, you ought to talk to your parents first, and tell them what you think about it. (France; B1 THRESHOLD; 2008; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form.
structures.example: Need you ask? (Greece; C2 MASTERY; 2002; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'ought to' without a following verb where the previous main verb is understood. ► ellipsis
structures.example: Otherwise some students would not get as much specialised help as they ought to. (Germany; B2 VANTAGE; 2010; German; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'needn't to' talk about a lack of obligation.
structures.example: I like summer so much because the weather is hot and we needn't wear a jacket. (Greece; B2 VANTAGE; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the question form rhetorically in discussion, typically in formal contexts.
structures.example: Need I go on? (Cyprus; C2 MASTERY; 2000; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the negative form.
structures.example: You needn't worry about where we can stay. (China; B2 VANTAGE; 1998; Chinese; Pass)

structures.guideword: FORM/USE: DESIRED STATES, WITH 'THERE OUGHT TO BE'
structures.can_do: Can use 'there ought to be' to talk about desired states of affairs.
structures.example: The rooms were dirty, there was no room service and there ought to be a lift since the rooms were on the 4th floor. (Sweden; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Swedish; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'ought to' to talk about desired states of affairs.
structures.example: Furthermore, we ought to take care of our health by going on trips to not unpolluted places as often as possible. (France; B2 VANTAGE; 1999; French; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'ought to' with 'really' to add emphasis.
structures.example: Moreover, you really ought to ask for details about the timetable they've set for schooling hours, just to be sure that its fits the with way of studying you are accustomed to. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2003; Greek; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'oughtn't' (without 'to') + verb.
structures.example: …they will most certainly have a banquet that day... and you oughtn't miss it for the world! (Portugal; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Portuguese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use 'shall I' to make offers.
structures.example: Shall I go and buy some cake and crackers? (Bulgarian, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2009)

structures.can_do: Can use 'ought to' to talk about something which is likely.
structures.example: … the fundamental function of accounting software is to record the numerous ordinary business activities, which may improve the efficiency of the company. Besides, it ought to provide useful information in decision-making. (China; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Chinese; Pass)

structures.can_do: Can use the affirmative form.
structures.example: We shall start tomorrow at 2 o'clock. (Marathi, A2 WAYSTAGE, Pass, 2006)
